rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the full elution window and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A midrange temperature leaves room to tune selectivity in either direction.

Change only gradient duration to measure whether the crowded central peaks respond to a shallower slope. The first run's short last retention time provides room to spread these pairs before the time penalty becomes substantial.

Raise the starting organic fraction to remove low-organic time, while using a slightly shallower slope than injection 2 to protect the critical central separation. This should bring the last peak close to 10 minutes without sacrificing full resolution.
Injection 3 already reaches the maximum CRF. Raise temperature one step to seek a shorter fully resolved separation while checking whether the critical pair retains its narrow resolution margin.

Test whether a larger temperature increase carries the critical pair through an elution-order reversal and restores resolution at shorter retention times. Keep injection 3 as the maximum-score reference while monitoring the neighboring pairs for new co-elutions.

Slightly flatten the gradient at 55 C to try to bring the new critical pair above R = 1.5 while preserving the recovered central separation. The last peak at 8.54 minutes leaves room for this adjustment without exceeding 10 minutes.

Test a narrower organic window to shorten the fully resolved 55 C method. The slope lies between injections 5 and 6; monitor both central critical pairs and the early peaks, which may become less retained at the higher starting organic fraction.

Restore the lower starting organic fraction to recover early and central separation, then use a slope midway between injections 5 and 6. This targets full resolution with the last peak near 9 minutes, shorter than either confirmed maximum-score method.

With the maximum CRF secured, test a cooler, steeper gradient for a potentially faster fully resolved separation. Lower temperature may improve the slope-sensitive central pair, but all neighboring pairs must be checked for selectivity changes.

At 55 C, lowering the starting organic fraction may improve the critical separation that deteriorated when phi0 was raised. Pair this with a steeper gradient to seek a fully resolved run shorter than injection 8, while retaining that maximum-score method as the reference.

Shorten injection 10 by one gradient-duration step to test the speed limit of this fully resolved selectivity window. Both critical pairs have modest margins, so retain injection 10 if either falls below R = 1.5.

Use an intermediate slope between injections 10 and 11 to recover the critical pair while shortening the fastest confirmed fully resolved separation. The reduced endpoint remains comfortably above the estimated organic fraction needed for the last peak.

Test a faster high-temperature regime where the troublesome middle pair may separate again after reversing elution order. This is an exploratory speed test; injection 12 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-score method.

Test whether further steepening increases separation of the middle pair in its reversed elution order at 60 C. Monitor neighboring pairs for compression while seeking a fully resolved separation substantially faster than injection 12.

Return to the promising 55 C regime and lower the starting organic fraction to improve the pair that limited injection 11. The steeper overall slope targets a shorter separation than injection 12, with particular attention to both central critical pairs.
Slightly flatten injection 15’s gradient to lift its limiting pair above R = 1.5 while targeting a last peak around 7.6 minutes. Check that the other central pair retains its small resolution margin.

Test an intermediate-temperature selectivity window that may permit a steeper gradient than the fully resolved 40 C method. This could shorten the separation, while avoiding the larger selectivity shifts that produced several unresolved pairs at 25 C.

Test a slightly steeper slope than injection 12 to locate the full-resolution boundary at phi0 = 0.10. This targets a last peak near 7.6 minutes; injection 16 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-score method.

Explore the remaining cooler selectivity window with a shallower slope than the unresolved 25 C and 35 C tests. This checks whether temperature-driven order changes can yield another fully resolved method below 10 minutes, while retaining injection 16 as the fastest confirmed maximum-score method.

Test whether 50 C combined with a steeper gradient provides a faster, fully resolved elution-order window. Injection 16 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-score method; monitor both central critical pairs closely.

Test whether a steeper gradient at 50 C improves the limiting central pair, using the lower starting organic fraction to help preserve its neighboring separation. This targets a faster selectivity window while retaining injection 16 as the fastest confirmed maximum-score method.

Refine the confirmed 40 C maximum-score method by raising phi0 one step, removing low-organic time while slightly flattening the gradient. Check whether the central critical pair remains resolved and the early peaks retain sufficient separation.

Refine the successful 55 C window with a slightly shallower slope than injection 12 to improve its limiting pair’s resolution margin. This should preserve maximum CRF with the last peak below 10 minutes; injection 16 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Preserve injection 16’s successful gradient slope while trimming the unused high-organic tail by two programmed minutes. All peaks should elute before the shortened gradient ends, retaining maximum CRF and the approximately 7.6-minute separation.

Use a slightly shallower slope than injection 8 to target larger margins for both critical pairs while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes. This tests a compact, maximum-score alternative; injections 16 and 24 remain the fastest confirmed fully resolved methods.
